sections.section_title: Early History and Evidences of Śiva Worship
sections.content:
The origin of Śaivism as a religion is lost in hoary and hazy antiquity. The earliest literary records in the country as well as the oldest archaeological finds suggest the prevalence of the worship of Śiva in some form or other. Leaving out references to it in the Vedic corpus and the evidences for it in the Indus Valley civilization, we find that Pāṇini (around 400 B.C.) not only knew Rudra but was acquainted that this god was also called Mṛḍā, Bhava and Sarva (1, 49; 3, 53; 4, 100). If we may believe Kalhaṇa's Rājataranginī, Aśoka (268-233 B.C.) visited Kāśhmir and erected a shrine to Śiva known as Aśokeśvara (1, 105-107). Kautilya prescribes that a temple to Śiva must be erected within the city (Sāma-śāstri's edition of Artha-sāstra, Book 2, Chapter 4, p.54). Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya (about 200 B.C.) makes an explicit reference to the people who were devoted exclusively to Śiva ('Śiva-bhāgavatas') (5, 2, 76). And the text also refers to the icons (arccā) of Śiva, Skanda and Viśākhā, which were being made and sold by the gold-seeking Mauryas: 
अपण्य इत्युच्यते तत्रेदं न सिध्यति ।
शिवं स्कन्दो विशाख इति ।
किं कारणं? मौर्यैर्हिरण्यार्थिभिरर्चाः प्रकल्पिताः ॥
It is probable that Śiva's worship in the form of liṅga had not yet come into vogue when Patañjali wrote his great commentary on Pāṇini. The bronze seal belonging to the first century B.C. found at Sirkāp site (Taxila) by John Marśal carries an iconic representation of Śiva, along with the legend 'Śiva-rakṣita' ("protected by Śiva") in Brāhmī and Kharōṣṭhī characters.
By the time the Gupta empire was formed (around 320 A.D.). The Śaiva religion had already become crystallized. One of the monarchs of this dynasty, Vainya-gupta, is recorded to have been a 'great devotee of Śiva'. The earliest mukha-linga (representation of Śiva in a liṅga but with the human face of Śiva carved in it) which was found at Khoh, belongs to the early Gupta period. The Vākāṭaka rulers (275-550 A.D.) Styled themselves with such titles as 'atyanta-māheśvara' and 'atyanta-svāmi-mahā-bhairava-bhakta', which indicate their zeal for the worship of śiva. Even the Ephthalite chieftain, Mihira-gula (515-535 A.D.) was a worshipper of Śiva as Paśupati. His coins bear a representation of bull as Śiva's insignia, with the legend "May victorious be the Bull". The kings of the North who wielded great influence after the Guptas, viz. the Maukharis, were also 'parama-māheśvaras'.
There is a suggestion that worship of Śiva was indigenous to South India. But it seems probable that Śaivism as a sect was first organized in Central India, and that it subsequently spread to Kāśmir and South India.
From the eighth to the twelth century A.D., Śaivism prevailed in Madhyapradesha, Kānya'ubja, Gujarat, Lāṭa and Kāśmīra. The major factor that moved the focus of Śaivism from Central India to Kāśmīra and South India was the uncertain political conditions in Central India.
Kāśmira was culturally a protected region, protected by nature and also by the strong and religious-minded monarchs and chieftains. It is small wonder that it took up the cause of Saivism and made it a valid and acceptable theology and metaphysics. In the South, the Pallava kings (325-897 A.D.) were zealous promoters of Śaiva religion, and so were the early Cāļukyas (543-745 A.D.). Śaivism as a sect gained great momentum during the days of the Cõļa emperors (846-1173 A.D.).
Thus, although the worship of Śiva may be one of the oldest and prehistoric cults in the world, Śaivism as an organized sect and creed is most probably a creature of the medieval period. Even before the eighth century, it must have been prevalent all over the country, for the Purāṇas uniformly mention Nepāla (Paśupati-nātha), Kedāra (Kedāreśvara), Vārāṇasī (Viśveśvara or Avimukta), Saurāṣṭra (Somanātha), Rāmeśvaram (Rāmanātha), Gokarṇa (Mahābaleśvara), Ujjayinī (Mahākāla), Gaṅgā-dvāra (Himālaya), Hemakūṭa (Virūpākṣa), Prabhāsa (Śāśi-śekhara), and Kāśmīra (Vijaya) as ancient and important centres of Śiva worship; and the Purāṇic accounts include several sites all over the country as especially sacred to Śiva. But how and when the religion was organized to have a doctrinal base and a sectarian superstructure, it is impossible to tell.
The traditional list of Śaiva-centres in the country are in five groups-viz. 'secret' (guhya), 'secret and beyond' (guhyati-guhya) and "exceeding secret' (atiguhya), "sacred ('pavitra') and enduring (sthānu), each group having eight centres of its own. The rationale of this classification is hard to figure out; but Sarva-jñānottara (Kriyā 8, 78) says that Śiva is manifested in the form of liṅgas in these places to benefit humanity. Kālottara (37, 23 f) counts as many as 68 spots sacred to Śiva.
अमरेशं प्रभासं नैमिषं पुष्करं तथा ।
आषाढी दण्डमुण्डि च भारभूति भवन्तिकम्।
लकुलीशश्च विख्याता गुह्याष्टकमुदाहृतम्।।
श्री पर्वतो हरिश्चन्द्रो जल्प्यमन्त्रादिकेश्वरम्।
मध्यमेशं महाकालं केदारं भैरवं तथा ॥
एतद् गुह्यातिगुह्यं च त्वष्टकं परिकीर्तितम् ।।
गया चैव कुरुक्षेत्रं नाखलं नखलं तथा।
विमलं चाट्टहासं च महेन्द्रं भीममष्टकम्।
अतिगुह्याष्टकं नाम सर्वपापप्रमोचनम्।।
छगलण्ड द्विरण्डं च माकोटमण्डलेश्वरः ।
कालांजनं शंखकर्णं स्थूलेश्वरस्थलेखरौ ।
पवित्राष्टकमित्येतन्महापुण्यविवर्धनम्।।
वस्त्रापदं रुद्रकोटिरमुक्तं महालयम् ।
गोकर्णं भद्रकर्णं च वर्णाक्षं चाति दीप्तिमान् ॥
स्थाण्वीश्वरं च विख्यातं त्रिषु लोकेषु विश्रुतम्।
स्थानाष्टकमिदं ज्ञेयं रुद्रक्षेत्र महोदयम्॥
(Śaivāgama-paribhāśā-mañjari, 8, 32-39)
Nor is it easy to reconstruct the early career of this organized religion. The available references in the philosophical and literary works of the medieval period point to the prevalence of several sects within Saivism such as Śaiva, Pāśupata, Kāruṇika-siddhāntin, Kāpālika, Mahā-vrata-dhara, Kāla-damana, Kālāmukha and Māheśvara. While it is extremely difficult to identify these sects in terms of their distinctive ideology, outlook, appearance, custom and conduct, it is likely that the differences between the sects were few and minor. Indeed, it would appear that the same sect was sometimes known by different names.
The Mahābhārata (śānti-parva, 349,) speaks only of Pāśupata as one of the doctrines (Jñāna) and sects (mata) prevalent in those days, others being Sāṁkhya, Yoga, Pāñca-rātra and Vaidika:
सांख्यं योगं पांचरात्र वदाः पाशुपतं तथा।
ज्ञानान्येतानि राजर्षे विद्धि नाना मतानि वै ॥
Probably Pāśupata was an all-inclusive expression; It was certainly the oldest among the sects. And it acquired celebrity not only by the doctrine it espoused, but by some strange practices that its adherents resorted to. The three major and influential divisions of Śaivism that emerged in the medieval period, viz. Kāśmir Śaivism, Tamil Śaivism, known as Śaiva-siddhānta and the Śaivism in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh known as Vīra-Śaiva, trace their origin alike to the Pāśupata sect which in turn places reliance on the Śaiva-āgamas.
Brahma-yāmala says that this form of Śaivism was taught by Śiva himself to Śrīkaṇṭha in Prayāga, and that this teaching was communicated by the latter to Bhairava and other disciples in 1,25,000 anuṣṭubh verses. In Kāśmir Śaivism, the belief is that the āgamas were revealed by Śiva as Śrīkaṇṭha to the sage Durvāsas, and that the latter taught the philosophy of non-dualism (abheda), dualism (bheda) and dualism-and-non-dualism (bhedābheda) to three of his disciples Tryambaka, Āmardaka and Śrīkaṇṭha respectively. Thus Śrīkaṇṭha (or Śrīkaṇṭha-nātha) appears to have been a historical figure, a human teacher very much associated with the crystallization or propagation of Śaivism in the early period.
sections.summary: This section traces the ancient origins of Śiva worship through literary and archaeological evidence, starting from Pāṇini (c. 400 B.C.) and Patañjali (c. 200 B.C.) to the Gupta period (c. 320 A.D.). It notes the existence of dedicated worshippers ('Śiva-bhāgavatas') and the commercial production of icons by the Mauryas. While Śiva worship is ancient and widespread, the author argues that Śaivism as an organized sect is a medieval development, likely originating in Central India and then spreading. The section lists numerous ancient Śaiva centers across India mentioned in the Purāṇas and identifies Pāśupata as the oldest and most inclusive sect, from which later major divisions like Kāśmir Śaivism, Śaiva-siddhānta, and Vīra-Śaiva emerged, all relying on the Śaiva-āgamas.

sections.content:
The mantle of this ancient teacher fell on Lakulīśa who appeared in Saurāṣṭra (Prabhāsa or Somanātha) and made Śaivism popular in Vārāṇasī, Dhāra, Māļvā, Kānyakubja and the present-day Rājāsthān.
(2)
Lakulīśa who has been hailed as an incarnation of Śiva himself (mūrtimān śamaras svayam) in Kāyāvarohaṇa in Bhṛgu-kacca (in Baroda State or-Saurāṣṭra) (Śrīmat-kāravantīrthe) was in all probability a historical figure; and his date is given as the first or the second century A.D.. He name is intimately associated with the Pāśupata variety of Śaivism. He is credited with having started a line of eighteen brilliant teachers who crystallized the Pāśupata sect and propagated it all over the country. Four among them are held in high regard, and are credited with having started their own lines of teaching (catuśśākhā): Kuśika, Gārgya, Maitreya and Karūśa.
His immediate disciple was Kauśika, who probably was the author of Pāśupata-sūtra, which book the tradition ascribes to Lakulīśa himself, and which is the definitive text of the Pāśupata system. The last teacher in the line, Kauṇ-ḍinya (also called Rāśi-kara), who lived sometime between the fourth and sixth centuries A.D., prepared a commentary on this text, called Pañcārtha-Bhāṣya. Bhāsarvajña's Ratna-ṭīkā (10th century) is a gloss on Haradatta's Gaṇa-kārikā, which establishes the link between the Pāśupata system and the Āgama literature.
These books are the main sources of the Pāśupata sect, which became very popular all over the country; and in course of time, the sect survived in two major factions: Kāpālika and Kālāmukha. It is surmised that the Spanda-faction of Kāśmir Śaivism contributed to the crystallization of the Kāpālika sub-set, while the Pratyabhijñā-faction was responsible for the Kālāmukha sub-set. The Kāpālikas degenerated into isolated tantrik cults while the Kālāmukhas gained popular favour by building temples and monastic settlements (maṭhas). The Kālāmukhas entered the Telugu country, and from Śrīśaila in Andhra Pradesh they entered Karnataka in the fifth or sixth century. And it became a dominant religious group between the ninth and thirteenth centuries, as upholders of Lakulīśa-Pāśupata doctrine (Lakulāgama-Samaya).
sections.summary: This section focuses on Lakulīśa, a historical figure from the 1st or 2nd century A.D., considered an incarnation of Śiva and the systematizer of the Pāśupata sect. It details his lineage of disciples, including Kuśika, Gārgya, Maitreya, and Karūśa, and key texts like the Pāśupata-sūtra and its commentaries. The Pāśupata sect eventually branched into two major factions, the Kāpālika and the Kālāmukha. The Kālāmukhas, unlike the Kāpālikas, gained popular support by establishing temples and monasteries (maṭhas), spreading from Śrīśaila into Karnataka and becoming a dominant religious force between the 9th and 13th centuries.

sections.section_title: The Kālāmukha Sect and its Influence in Karnataka
sections.content:
The two major divisions of the Kālāmukha (Pāśupata) subject are recognised as 'śakti-parṣe' and "simhaparse' in the Kannaḍa country. The 'parṣhes' (the Kannaḍa version of the Sanskrit pariśad, meaning assembly or congregation) were territorial jurisdictions. The former had two sub-divisions, one owing direct allegiance to Śrī-śaila ('Parvatāvali') or 'Parvatāmnāya') and the other calling itself 'Bhujaṅgāvali' (the line founded by Bhujaṅga-Deva). The former appears to have prevailed in Karnataka. There is a Kannaḍa inscription of 1057 A.D. from Karnūl (in Andhra Pradesh), which refers to one Sureśvara-paṇḍita-deva, "the royal swan in the pond of the Kālāmukha sect", ("Kālāmukha-samaya-sarovara-rājahamsar"), "veritably the sun for the water-lily of the Lākula doctrines and arguments" ("lākula-siddhānta-naiyāyika-nalini-divākarar"), "the western decorative arch for Śrī-śaila" (Śrī-śaila paścima-dvāra-toraṇar") and "person instrumental for obtaining a sight of God Mallikārjuna” (“mallikārjuna-deva-darśana-kāraṇa-puruśar"). This inscription not only identifies the Kālāmukha sect with the sect founded by Lākula, but suggests that the sect spread in the western direction (viz. towards Karnataka) from Śrī-śaila.
The Kālāmukhas became predominant in the Tamil country also. Thus in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nādu, the temples and monastic settlements were largely owing to the Kālāmukha interest. In other parts of the country also, the Pāśupatas had encouraged the building of the temples, which they themselves administered. As early as 610-639 A.D., we have an inscription which records the grant of a village (Aigaṭapuri) to the temple of Kapāleśvara in Nāsik district. The inscription also mentions the "mahāvrati" ascetics (Kālāmukha) who lived in the temple and looked after the interests of the temple. The Rāṣṭrakūṭa monarch Kṛṣṇa III (about 958 A.D.) in his Karhaḍ inscription makes over a village to Gaṅga-śiva, who is described as an "ascetic" (tapasvi) and as the "emperor of the architects of the śaiva-sect" (śaivasiddhānta-nirmāpaṇa-sārvabhauma). He was a disciple of Īśāna-śiva, who was the chief of the Valkalīśvara-maṭha (monastic settlement attached to a temple) in Karahaṭa. The monarch Kīrtivarman got constructed a pavillion in the Nīlakaṇṭha temple at Kālañjara (on the hill in Bundelkhand) at the instance of his preceptor Śrī-mūrti, who was a Pāśupata ascetic (in Vikrama Samvatsara 1147). Numerous temples in North India owe their origin to Pāśupata encouragement.
(3)
That the cult named after Lakulīśa was popular in Karnataka by 600 A.D. is evident from the sculpture of Lakulīśa carved in the Mahākuṭa temple, to which temple Durlabhā-devī made land-grants as mentioned in the inscription of the Cāḷukyan king, Maṅgalīśa (596-610 A.D.). There was a separate shrine to Lakulīśa in Bādāmī about the same time. And by 640 A.D., Nandi near Bangalore appears to have been an important centre of this sect, for an inscription dated 640 A.D. refers to a maṭha of the Kālāmukhas, whose head was one Kālaśakti (to whose disciple, Īśvaradeva by name, Ratnāvaḷī, mother of a Bāṇa king, made a grant). The famous temple at Nandi was built by the Noḷamba kings, who being staunch Śaivites, patronized the Lākula sect. They claimed to be pillars of the Lākula doctrine and practice ('lākula-samaya-stamba'). These kings who claimed to be scions of the Pallava family, had ruled over parts of Karnataka from the eighth to the eleventh centuries with Heñjeru (Hemāvati, now in Anantapur district of Andhra Pradesh) as their capital. It was during their rule that Nandi rose to prominence, as also Āvani (in Kolar district where they built the well-known Lakṣmaṇeśvara temple), not to mention Heñjeru (where they built the Doddeśvara or Noḷambeśvara temple and Siddeśvara, Virūpākṣa and Malleśvara temples). The great warrior king, Mahendra (870-897 A.D.), who styled himself a "parama-māheśvara", dedicated his own palace to Mahādeva (viz. Śiva), and installed Mahendreśvara therein, granting generous gifts to the shrine.
sections.summary: This section details the organization and spread of the Kālāmukha sect, a branch of Pāśupata Śaivism, particularly its strong presence in Karnataka by 600 A.D. It describes the sect's divisions, like 'śakti-parṣe' and 'siṁhaparse', and its lineages, such as 'Parvatāvali' from Śrīśaila. The section provides extensive inscriptional and architectural evidence of Kālāmukha influence, including royal patronage from dynasties like the Cāḷukyas, Rāṣṭrakūṭas, and especially the Noḷambas, who were staunch patrons and built numerous temples in centers like Nandi, Āvani, and their capital Heñjeru. The Kālāmukhas were instrumental in building and administering temples across South and North India.

sections.section_title: Temple Culture, Fusion with other Cults, and Decline
sections.content:
The Lākula-Śaivas, who prevailed till the fifteenth century, made a profound impact on the religious life of South India. In particular, they were responsible for building temples in almost every village in the area, and providing a new dimension to the temple-culture.
The teachers of this faith were very well organised into 'maṭhas', and encouraged Sanskrit learning (especially the Vedic lore, because they called themselves "śruti-mukhya" or adorers of the Vedas) and ethical living. These maṭhas were invariably attached to temples, and the expression 'deva-sthāna' for the temple became popular under their influence. The temple was where the god's icon was installed and worshipped (deva), and also where the Lākula teachers resided along with their celibate disciples (sthāna). As administrators of the temples and principals of the schools attached to these temples, they were called 'sthāna-patis' or 'sthānikas'. Heñjēru, the Noḷamba capital, had a large university ('śrīmatu-heñjeru-paṭṭaṇada mahā-ghaṭikā-sthāna') attached to the Noḷambeśvara temple, over which Ananta-śiva-deva presided as 'ācārya-rāja-guru'.
The Kedāreśvara temple at Balligāme (in Shivamogga district) founded by the Kālāmukha teacher, Kedāra-śakti, on the banks of a pond called Tāvare-kere, had a 'maṭha' (cloister and college) attached to it. This was called 'Kōḍiya-maṭha' or 'Kedāra-sthāna'. It flourished at any rate from 1078 till 1215 A.D. if inscriptions are any clue. There is an inscription dated 1162 A.D. which describes the functions of this "maṭha": it provided teaching in the four vedas, Sanskrit grammar, different branches of philosophy, the purāṇas, poetry, drama and other aspects of literature; it provided free food for the poor, the destitute and the physically handicapped, and also for the professional musicians, dancers and actors, and for mendicants and strangers to the town; and medical treatment and nursing were offered free for the sick who were poor and who had none to look after; and it was "a place of assurance of safety for all living creatures” (EC, VII SK 102, tr. by Fleet, El, 5,222, cited in David N. Lorenzen, The Kāpālikas and Kālāmukhas, pp. 103-104).
There were several temples also in the Belgaum area (like Andhāsura temple at Hūli, Jagadīśvara temple at Munavalli, Malleśvara temple at Belgaum, Mallikārjuna temple at Saundaṭṭi), Bellary (like Dakṣiṇa-someśvara temple at Tumbuḷ, Svayambhū temple at Kuragōḍu, and Malleśvara temple at Siṇḍigeri), Bijāpur (like Syayambhū-siddeśvara temple and Śiva-liṅga-deva temple at Muṭṭagi), Dhārwāḍ (like Brahmeśvara temple, now called Basaveśvara temple, at Ablur, and temples at Hoṁbaḷ, Gadagu and Lakṣmeśvara), and Hassan (like the Kālāmukha temples at Haḷebīḍu, Gajeśvara temple at Arasikere, Kalledeva tempie at Jājūr, Jagateśvara temple at Kanikaṭṭa) districts in Karnataka. Most of these temples were built under the patronage of the Kalyāṇa Cāḷukya kings, especially of 'Bhuvanaika-malla' Someśvara II (1068-1076), who was a zealous Śaiva, and of his successor, Tribhuvana-malla' Pērmāḍi-Vikramāditya VI (1706-1127), who notwithstanding being a Jaina by personal conviction, extended patronage to the Kālāmukha shrines.
Although the Kālāmukhas were fervent Śaivas, they were not fanatical. They not only tolerated but actively encouraged other faiths and sects. They supported the learning of the four Vedas, and were themselves Vaidika in general inclination. They also imparted in their schools instruction in such varied disciplines like Nyāya, Sāṁkhya, Buddhism, Mīmāṁsā and Yoga. One of the Kālāmukha teachers, Someśvara, who administered the Nagareśvara temple and college at Sūḍi (Dhārwāḍ district), is described in an inscription of 1075 A.D., as a Buddha to the Buddhist, a Jina to the Jains, an Akṣapāda (Gotama) to the Naiyāyika, a Kaṇāda to the Vaiśeṣika, a Jaimini to the Mīmāṁsaka and a Bṛhaspati to the grammarian.
Keśirāja-daṇḍādhīśa (Keśimayya), who was minister to Bijjaḷa II (1130-1167), and had the great Kālāmukha master and 'rājaguru', Vāmaśakti-dēva as his 'ārādhya' (revered family-priest and mentor), built a temple to Keśava in the southern quarters of Balligāme and provided a 'brahma-pura' (residential quarters for learned brahmins) attached to the temple. A branch of the Kālāmukha ascetics was devoted to Mahālakṣmī of Kolhāpur. Because of the receptivity of the Kālāmukhas, the Pāśupata cult from Kāśmīr could not only enter Karnataka but make an impact upon the indigenous Śaiva ideology; the Nātha-siddha votaries from Nepāl could settle down in Karnataka and contribute to the merger of Buddhism in Śaivism.
(4)
The advent and influence of the Nātha-siddha cult in the ninth century and its fusion with Śaivism of the Kālāmukha persuasion are best illustrated in the coastal region of Karnataka. Besides the well-known Kadari hill in Mangalore (where a vihāra was built as early 968 A.D.) there were several centres of this cult; important among them being Candrapuri (Candāvara, Honnāvar taluk; 11th century), Bārakūru (1140), Basarūru (12th century), Mundukūru (Kārkaḷa taluk; around 1293), Koṭeśvara (around 1372) and Viṭṭala (Banṭwāḷa taluk; as late as 1531). Common settlements of the 'jogis' belonging to this cult as well as to the Kālāmukha sect (-an inscription of 1372 records charity for feeding 'ubhaya-jaṅgamas' in the temple of Koṭeśvara-) were found in several places like Koṭeśvara, Viṭṭala, Ambūru, Maṅgalapāḍi (Kāsargoḍ taluk), Bārakūru and Addūru (Mangalore). The worship of Lokeśvara, Bhairava, Vīrabhadra, Mañjunātha, Gorakhnāth, Hiṅgulā-devī, Nakhareśvara and several Jogi-puruśas (like Jugādikuṇḍala-jogi-puruśa and Sadānanda-jogi) in this region is ascribable to the confluence of the Nātha-siddha and Kālāmukha ideologies and practices.
The Kālāmukha administration of temples made the temple in the town or village a socio-economic organization, in addition to its being a religious and educational institution. Popular entertainment (music, dance and drama) was included in the ritual sequences of temples. This is an application of the Pāśupata prescription that among the observances of the Pāśupata devotee (vidhi) must be included the six-fold 'niyama'. The first two aspects of the niyama are music (gīta) and dance (nṛtta), followed by laughter (hasana), making weird and repetitive sounds like drum-beating (huḍukkāra), prostrations (namaskāra) and repetition of divine names (japa). We have an inscription of uncertain date mentioning a land-donation to a dancing girl (sūḷe) of the Tripurāntaka temple at Balligāme made by the Kālāmukha priest of the temple, Trilocana-munīndra of Bhujaṅgāvali lineage, which suggests that the temple prostitution (devadāsī) was a feature of the temples administered by the Kālāmukhas (David N. Lorenzen, op. cit. p. 139-140). The mention of temple-prostitutes occurs not earlier than 778 A.D.; in an inscription of that date in the Vīrūpākṣa temple at Paṭṭadakallu is the first mention. In subsequent years, inscriptions do occasionally mention actors (pātra) and prostitutes ('dēgulada sūḷe') attached to temple, to discharge the duties of 'nṛtta' (dance), 'gīta' (songs) and 'vādya' (instrumental music). The custom appears to have gathered strength from the tenth century onwards. In 1058, Nāgadevayya who got the Nāgeśvara temple built in Sūndi also got a township built for the temple prostitutes in the vicinity of that temple (El, 15 p.8).
The sect seems to have lost its importance during the period 1160-1200 A.D., although it continued to figure in inscriptions as late as 1410 A.D. The Rājaguru of Harihara I (1336-1356) and Bukka (1356-1377) was a Kālāmukha teacher, Kāśivilāsa-kriyāśakti by name. The Virūpākṣa temple at Hampi was probably administered by this teacher. The shrine to Vidyāśaṅkara at Śṛṅgeri was built, according to an inscription of 1390 A.D. in memory of (or 'with the permission of, as another reading of the words in the inscription would have it) this teacher. But after this period, the influence of the Kālāmukha teachers appears to have waned.
But the major factor which pushed the Kālāmukha impact to the background was the rise of the Vīraśaiva movement spearheaded by Basava, who was treasurer to the Kalacūri-Bijjaḷa of Kalyāṇa (1130-1167). But it was the Kālāmukha sect that provided the backdrop for the Vīraśaiva creed, and it has been suggested that the latter was a reformist movement growing out of the former (Lorenzen, op. cit., p. 167). But the two creeds had different social and philosophical orientations. The Kālāmuk-has, however, lost their ground in Karnataka after the advent of Basaveśvara and were gradually absorbed within the Vīraśaiva fold. Many of the Kālāmukha shrines in later years came under the control of the Vīraśaivas, like the Kedāreśvara temple at Balligāme, the Trikūṭeśvara temple at Gadagu (in Dhārwāḍ district), the Brahmeśvara temple at Ablūr (in Dhārwād district, now called Basaveśvara temple) and the Kālāmukha 'maṭha' at Hūli (in Belgāum district).
sections.summary: This section explores the profound impact of the Lākula-Śaivas (Kālāmukhas) on South Indian religious life. It highlights their role in establishing temples and attached monasteries ('maṭhas') which served as centers for Vedic learning, education in various philosophies, and extensive social welfare, including free food and medical care. The Kālāmukhas were tolerant, encouraging other faiths and fusing with other cults like the Nātha-siddhas, as seen in coastal Karnataka. Their temple administration incorporated entertainment (music, dance) and controversially, temple prostitution ('devadāsī'). The section concludes by detailing the decline of the Kālāmukhas between 1160-1200 A.D., primarily due to the rise of the Vīraśaiva movement under Basava, which eventually absorbed many Kālāmukha followers and institutions.
key_concepts: Maṭhas as educational and social centers

chapter_summary: This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of the history of Śaivism. It begins by establishing the ancient, prehistoric origins of Śiva worship, citing early literary texts like those of Pāṇini and Patañjali, and archaeological findings. The author argues that while the cult of Śiva is ancient, its formal organization into a religion with distinct sects is a medieval phenomenon, likely originating in Central India. A key figure in this process was Lakulīśa (c. 1st-2nd century A.D.), who systematized the Pāśupata sect, the oldest and most foundational branch of Śaivism. The chapter then focuses on the Pāśupata sub-sect, the Kālāmukhas, who became a dominant religious force in South India, particularly in Karnataka, from the 9th to the 13th centuries. Supported by royal patronage, the Kālāmukhas were prolific temple-builders and established monasteries ('maṭhas') that served as major centers for education, social welfare, and cultural activities. The chapter also discusses the Kālāmukhas' syncretic nature, absorbing elements from other traditions like the Nātha-siddha cult. Finally, it details the decline of the Kālāmukha influence around the 12th century, largely due to the rise of the Vīraśaiva movement led by Basava, which absorbed many of the Kālāmukha centers and followers.
key_arguments: While the worship of Śiva is of 'hoary and hazy antiquity,' Śaivism as an organized sectarian religion is a product of the medieval period.
The Pāśupata sect, systematized by the historical figure Lakulīśa, is the foundational sect from which later major Śaiva divisions emerged.

The Kālāmukha sub-sect played a crucial role in the proliferation of Śaivism in South India, particularly Karnataka, through extensive temple building and the establishment of influential monastic centers (maṭhas).
Kālāmukha-administered temples were not just religious sites but also comprehensive socio-economic, educational, and cultural institutions.
The decline of the Kālāmukhas was precipitated by the rise of the Vīraśaiva movement, which ultimately absorbed many of their institutions and followers.
key_takeaways: Śaivism's history is characterized by a transition from an ancient, amorphous cult to a structured, sectarian religion in the medieval era.
Lakulīśa is a pivotal historical figure in the formalization of Śaiva doctrine.
The Kālāmukhas were instrumental in shaping the religious, social, and cultural landscape of medieval South India, especially through their development of temple-centric communities.

The religious history of India involves complex processes of fusion and absorption between different sects, as seen in the Kālāmukha interaction with the Nātha-siddhas and their eventual assimilation into Vīraśaivism.

historical_figures.name: Pāṇini
historical_figures.significance: His work shows acquaintance with Śiva's names (Mṛḍā, Bhava, Sarva), indicating the god's worship in his time.

historical_figures.name: Aśoka
historical_figures.significance: According to Kalhaṇa's Rājataranginī, he visited Kāśhmir and erected a shrine to Śiva called Aśokeśvara.

historical_figures.name: Kalhaṇa
historical_figures.significance: His work, Rājataranginī, is cited as the source for Aśoka's connection to Śaivism in Kashmir.

historical_figures.name: Kautilya
historical_figures.significance: Prescribed that a temple to Śiva must be erected within the city.

historical_figures.name: Patañjali
historical_figures.significance: Made explicit reference to 'Śiva-bhāgavatas' (devotees of Śiva) and the selling of Śiva icons by the Mauryas.

historical_figures.name: John Marśal
historical_figures.significance: Found a 1st century B.C. bronze seal at Sirkāp (Taxila) with an iconic representation of Śiva.

historical_figures.name: Vainya-gupta
historical_figures.significance: Recorded as being a 'great devotee of Śiva', indicating the religion's crystallization by the Gupta era.

historical_figures.name: Mihira-gula
historical_figures.significance: Was a worshipper of Śiva as Paśupati; his coins featured Śiva's bull insignia.

historical_figures.name: Śrīkaṇṭha
historical_figures.significance: Believed in some traditions to have received the Śaiva teachings directly from Śiva and transmitted them to disciples. Appears to have been a historical figure.

historical_figures.name: Bhairava
historical_figures.significance: Received the Śaiva teachings from Śrīkaṇṭha.

historical_figures.name: Durvāsas
historical_figures.significance: In Kāśmir Śaivism, believed to have received the āgamas from Śiva (as Śrīkaṇṭha) and taught different philosophical paths to his disciples.

historical_figures.name: Tryambaka, Āmardaka and Śrīkaṇṭha
historical_figures.significance: Taught the philosophies of non-dualism (abheda), dualism (bheda), and dualism-and-non-dualism (bhedābheda) respectively.

historical_figures.name: Lakulīśa
historical_figures.significance: A key historical figure who systematized and propagated Pāśupata Śaivism. Hailed as an incarnation of Śiva.

historical_figures.name: Kuśika, Gārgya, Maitreya, Karūśa
historical_figures.significance: Four highly regarded disciples who started their own lines of teaching (catuśśākhā).

historical_figures.name: Kauśika
historical_figures.significance: Probable author of the Pāśupata-sūtra, the definitive text of the system.

historical_figures.name: Kauṇḍinya (Rāśi-kara)
historical_figures.significance: Prepared the Pañcārtha-Bhāṣya, a commentary on the Pāśupata-sūtra.

historical_figures.name: Bhāsarvajña
historical_figures.significance: Wrote the Ratna-ṭīkā, a gloss on Haradatta's Gaṇa-kārikā, linking the Pāśupata system to Āgama literature.

historical_figures.name: Haradatta
historical_figures.significance: Wrote the Gaṇa-kārikā.

historical_figures.name: Bhujaṅga-Deva
historical_figures.significance: Founded the 'Bhujaṅgāvali' lineage of the Kālāmukha sect.

historical_figures.name: Sureśvara-paṇḍita-deva
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a 1057 A.D. inscription, linking the Kālāmukha sect to Lākula's doctrines and the Śrīśaila center.

historical_figures.name: Kṛṣṇa III
historical_figures.significance: His Karhaḍ inscription records a land grant to a Śaiva ascetic, showing royal patronage.

historical_figures.name: Gaṅga-śiva
historical_figures.significance: Recipient of a land grant from Kṛṣṇa III, described as a leader in the Śaiva sect.

historical_figures.name: Īśāna-śiva
historical_figures.significance: Preceptor of Gaṅga-śiva.

historical_figures.name: Kīrtivarman
historical_figures.significance: Constructed a pavilion in the Nīlakaṇṭha temple at the instance of his Pāśupata preceptor.

historical_figures.name: Śrī-mūrti
historical_figures.significance: Preceptor of King Kīrtivarman.

historical_figures.name: Durlabhā-devī
historical_figures.significance: Made land grants to the Mahākuṭa temple.

historical_figures.name: Maṅgalīśa
historical_figures.significance: His inscription mentions the land grants of Durlabhā-devī, confirming early Śaiva activity in Karnataka.

historical_figures.name: Kālaśakti
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a 640 A.D. inscription at Nandi, indicating an early Kālāmukha center.

historical_figures.name: Ratnāvaḷī
historical_figures.significance: Made a grant to Kālaśakti's disciple, showing patronage.

historical_figures.name: Īśvaradeva
historical_figures.significance: Recipient of a grant from Ratnāvaḷī.

historical_figures.name: Mahendra
historical_figures.significance: A great warrior king and 'parama-māheśvara' who dedicated his palace to Śiva.

historical_figures.name: Ananta-śiva-deva
historical_figures.significance: Presided over the large university attached to the Noḷambeśvara temple at Heñjeru.

historical_figures.name: Kedāra-śakti
historical_figures.significance: Founded the Kedāreśvara temple and Kōḍiya-maṭha at Balligāme.

historical_figures.name: Someśvara II ('Bhuvanaika-malla')
historical_figures.significance: A zealous Śaiva who patronized Kālāmukha shrines.

historical_figures.name: Pērmāḍi-Vikramāditya VI ('Tribhuvana-malla')
historical_figures.significance: Although a Jaina, he extended patronage to Kālāmukha shrines. The dates 1706-1127 are a clear typographical error in the source text; the correct reign is 1076-1127.

historical_figures.name: Someśvara
historical_figures.significance: Administered the Nagareśvara temple at Sūḍi and was praised in an inscription for his broad learning and tolerance.

historical_figures.name: Bijjaḷa II
historical_figures.significance: His minister, Keśirāja, was a patron of the Kālāmukha sect. He was also the king whom Basava served.

historical_figures.name: Keśirāja-daṇḍādhīśa (Keśimayya)
historical_figures.significance: Follower of the Kālāmukha master Vāmaśakti-dēva, built a temple to Keśava.

historical_figures.name: Vāmaśakti-dēva
historical_figures.significance: Was the revered preceptor ('ārādhya') of minister Keśirāja.

historical_figures.name: Trilocana-munīndra
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in an inscription as making a land donation to a dancing girl, suggesting Kālāmukha involvement with the devadāsī system.

historical_figures.name: Nāgadevayya
historical_figures.significance: Built the Nāgeśvara temple at Sūndi and a township for temple prostitutes.

historical_figures.name: Harihara I
historical_figures.significance: His Rājaguru was the Kālāmukha teacher Kāśivilāsa-kriyāśakti.

historical_figures.name: Bukka
historical_figures.significance: His Rājaguru was the Kālāmukha teacher Kāśivilāsa-kriyāśakti.

historical_figures.name: Kāśivilāsa-kriyāśakti
historical_figures.significance: Was the Rājaguru of Harihara I and Bukka, administered the Virūpākṣa temple at Hampi, and was honored by the Vidyāśaṅkara shrine at Śṛṅgeri.

historical_figures.name: Basava
historical_figures.significance: Spearheaded the Vīraśaiva movement, which led to the decline of the Kālāmukhas and their absorption into the new creed.

historical_events.event: Creation of a bronze seal with Śiva's image and the name 'Śiva-rakṣita'.
historical_events.significance: Early archaeological evidence of iconic representation of Śiva.

historical_events.event: Life of Lakulīśa, founder of the Pāśupata sect.
historical_events.significance: Pivotal moment in the systematization of Śaivism as a formal philosophical and religious system.

historical_events.event: Formation of the Gupta Empire; crystallization of Śaiva religion.
historical_events.significance: Śaivism becomes a more established and formally recognized religion, with royal patronage.

historical_events.event: Creation of the earliest known mukha-linga at Khoh.
historical_events.significance: Development in Śaiva iconography, combining aniconic and iconic forms.

historical_events.event: Vākāṭaka rulers adopt Śaiva titles.
historical_events.significance: Demonstrates the deep integration of Śaivism with royal identity in the Deccan.

historical_events.event: Life of Kauṇḍinya, Pāśupata commentator.
historical_events.significance: Development of scholastic tradition within the Pāśupata sect.

historical_events.event: Kālāmukhas enter Karnataka from Śrīśaila.
historical_events.significance: Beginning of the sect's expansion and eventual dominance in the South.

historical_events.event: Reign of Maṅgalīśa; inscriptions show patronage to Śaiva temples.
historical_events.significance: Early evidence of the Lākula cult's popularity in Karnataka.

historical_events.event: Inscription records a village grant to Kapāleśvara temple and mentions Kālāmukha ascetics.
historical_events.significance: Early evidence of Kālāmukhas administering temples.

historical_events.event: Inscription refers to a Kālāmukha maṭha at Nandi.
historical_events.significance: Shows the establishment of Kālāmukha monastic centers in Karnataka.

historical_events.event: First known inscriptional mention of temple-prostitutes (devadāsīs).
historical_events.significance: Marks the beginning of the recorded history of a controversial but long-standing temple practice.

historical_events.event: Advent of the Nātha-siddha cult in Karnataka.
historical_events.significance: Led to the fusion of Nātha-siddha and Kālāmukha ideologies, particularly in coastal regions.

historical_events.event: Karhaḍ inscription of Kṛṣṇa III records a grant to a Śaiva ascetic.
historical_events.significance: Example of Rāṣṭrakūṭa royal patronage for the Śaiva sect.

historical_events.event: A vihāra (Buddhist monastery) was built on Kadari hill, Mangalore.
historical_events.significance: Indicates the presence of multiple religious traditions in a region later known for the fusion of Buddhism and Śaivism.

historical_events.event: Kannaḍa inscription from Karnūl describes the Kālāmukha teacher Sureśvara-paṇḍita-deva.
historical_events.significance: Provides details on the identity and spread of the Kālāmukha sect.

historical_events.event: Nāgadevayya builds the Nāgeśvara temple and a township for prostitutes at Sūndi.
historical_events.significance: Shows the institutionalization of temple prostitution under Śaiva patronage.

historical_events.event: Flourishing period of the Kōḍiya-maṭha at Balligāme.
historical_events.significance: Represents the peak of Kālāmukha monastic centers as hubs of education and social welfare.

historical_events.event: Reign of Kalacūri-Bijjaḷa of Kalyāṇa.
historical_events.significance: The political context for the rise of Basava and the Vīraśaiva movement.

historical_events.event: Period of decline for the Kālāmukha sect.
historical_events.significance: Marks a major shift in the religious landscape of Karnataka with the rise of Vīraśaivism.

historical_events.event: An inscription describes the multifaceted functions of the Kōḍiya-maṭha.
historical_events.significance: Provides a detailed primary source account of the socio-educational role of a Kālāmukha monastery.

historical_events.event: Reigns of Harihara I and Bukka of Vijayanagara.
historical_events.significance: The Kālāmukha sect still held influence, with its teachers serving as royal preceptors (Rājaguru).

historical_events.event: Inscription records charity for feeding 'ubhaya-jaṅgamas' (both Nātha-siddha and Kālāmukha ascetics).
historical_events.significance: Evidence of the co-existence and fusion of the two sects.

historical_events.event: Vidyāśaṅkara shrine at Śṛṅgeri is built in connection with the Kālāmukha teacher Kāśivilāsa-kriyāśakti.
historical_events.significance: Shows the continued prestige of Kālāmukha teachers even as the sect's general influence was waning.

historical_events.event: Kālāmukhas continue to be mentioned in inscriptions.
historical_events.significance: Indicates the sect's lingering presence long after its peak.

quotations.quote:
अमरेशं प्रभासं नैमिषं पुष्करं तथा ।
आषाढी दण्डमुण्डि च भारभूति भवन्तिकम्।
लकुलीशश्च विख्याता गुह्याष्टकमुदाहृतम्।।
श्री पर्वतो हरिश्चन्द्रो जल्प्यमन्त्रादिकेश्वरम्।
मध्यमेशं महाकालं केदारं भैरवं तथा ॥
एतद् गुह्यातिगुह्यं च त्वष्टकं परिकीर्तितम् ।।
गया चैव कुरुक्षेत्रं नाखलं नखलं तथा।
विमलं चाट्टहासं च महेन्द्रं भीममष्टकम्।
अतिगुह्याष्टकं नाम सर्वपापप्रमोचनम्।।
छगलण्ड द्विरण्डं च माकोटमण्डलेश्वरः ।
कालांजनं शंखकर्णं स्थूलेश्वरस्थलेखरौ ।
पवित्राष्टकमित्येतन्महापुण्यविवर्धनम्।।
वस्त्रापदं रुद्रकोटिरमुक्तं महालयम् ।
गोकर्णं भद्रकर्णं च वर्णाक्षं चाति दीप्तिमान् ॥
स्थाण्वीश्वरं च विख्यातं त्रिषु लोकेषु विश्रुतम्।
स्थानाष्टकमिदं ज्ञेयं रुद्रक्षेत्र महोदयम्॥

images_and_diagrams.description: A blurry, circular, greyish graphic element is visible on the edge of most pages. It appears to be a decorative part of the book's design and is not referenced in the text.

controversial_points: The author qualifies the story of Aśoka building a Śiva shrine with 'If we may believe Kalhaṇa's Rājataranginī,' suggesting its historicity may be debated.

The origin of organized Śaivism is presented as a debatable point, with the author countering the 'suggestion that worship of Śiva was indigenous to South India' with the probability that it 'was first organized in Central India.'

The relationship between the Kālāmukha sect and the Vīraśaiva movement is noted as a point of discussion. The text mentions it 'has been suggested that the latter was a reformist movement growing out of the former' but immediately adds that 'the two creeds had different social and philosophical orientations,' questioning a simple linear development.
The text links the Kālāmukha sect to the practice of temple prostitution ('devadāsī'), which is a sensitive and debated topic in the study of Indian religious history.

alternative_viewpoints.viewpoint: The worship of Śiva was indigenous to South India.
alternative_viewpoints.presented_as: A suggestion mentioned in the text, which the author contrasts with his own thesis that organized Śaivism originated in Central India.

alternative_viewpoints.viewpoint: The Vīraśaiva creed was a reformist movement that grew out of the Kālāmukha sect.
alternative_viewpoints.presented_as: A suggestion attributed to scholar David Lorenzen, which the author seems to temper by highlighting the different social and philosophical orientations of the two sects.
